newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia plays down early campaign tensions.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia plays down early campaign tensions.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar party pressed ahead with an election rally on Saturday and the government played down disturbances that marred the first week of campaigning.

The minority United Development Party (PPP) and Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) cancelled campaigning this week in key cities on the main island of Java after clashes, and a PPP official described the central city of Yogyakarta as tense.
But the official Antara news agency quoted Interior Minister Yogie Memet as saying: "Boycotts or other disturbances are common and do not need to be exaggerated."
Memet also heads the national General Election Institute (LPU) which is running the May 29 polls in the world's fourth most populous nation of 200 million people.
The Moslem-oriented PPP, one of only three parties allowed to contest the elections, this week halted campaigning in Yogyakarta after windows at its party headquarters there were smashed.
"The city is actually tense, even though things seem to go on quite well. I think disturbances may erupt anytime," Suwandi Subroto, a deputy secretary of the PPP's Yogyakarta branch, said.
Subroto said party officials would meet on Monday to decide whether to continue the campaign, which will last through May 23.
"What we are doing now is cooling down. There's no use in continuing to hold the campaign when (our) people are burning with emotion," he told Reuters.
On Friday, the PPP cancelled five rallies in Jakarta after it said police had refused permission for a meeting to be addressed by the party's leader.
Jakarta police said the permit the PPP had sought did not match a previous agreement between the party and security agencies.

Despite the cancellation, thousands of PPP supporters took to the streets of the capital on Friday in illegal convoys of motorcyles and other vehicles in open violation of strict campaign regulations. Police did not confront the rallies.
Jakarta was quiet on Saturday, a Golkar campaigning day, as heavy rain dampened campaign outdoor events.
A rally led by Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita ended prematurely -- it was washed out when a heavy rainstorm short-circuited the public address system and ended a pop music performance.
Party chiefs placated the restless crowd of about 3,000 people by throwing free T-shirts, other clothing and 10,000 rupiah ($4.11) notes to youthful supporters at the stage front.
Clashes between supporters of rival parties have also been reported in other districts in Central Java province, especially around the northern coastal town of Pekalongan.
In Indonesia's second city of Surabaya the PDI stopped campaigning after it had to cancel a rally following a clash between supporters of two rival factions on Monday.
The three legal parties, the PPP, the ruling Golkar and the PDI, have agreed to campaign on different days in different parts of the country to avoid violence.
They are vying for the backing of nearly 125 million voters to fill 425 elected seats in the 500-seat House of Representatives. The other seats are allotted to the military, which does not vote.
Golkar, in power for the past 30 years under President Suharto's rule, is seeking to push its share of the vote over 70 percent from the 68 percent it won in the last polls in 1992.
The PPP won 17 percent and the PDI 15.
